INT301 International Law and World Politics · Week 4

Force and Existence

Week 4: International law and the use of force by states. One reading defends the post-1945 prohibition on force as it collapses. The other asks what the Genocide Convention's promise of a group's right to exist means for a people shaped by law as a racialized group.

  • 2 readings
  • 43 pages
  • 10 headed sections
  • 30 self-test questions
READING 1 · ESSAY · PP. 80–93

Might Unmakes Right

Oona A. Hathaway and Scott J. Shapiro, “Might Unmakes Right: The Catastrophic Collapse of Norms Against the Use of Force”, Foreign Affairs, July/August 2025, pp. 80–93.

Before 1928 war was lawful and “might made right”. The Kellogg–Briand Pact and the UN Charter outlawed conquest, and this, more than deterrence or democracy, produced eight decades of rare interstate war, freer trade and sanctions-based (“outcasting”) enforcement, all resting on the expectation that violators (especially under US leadership) would pay. Trump's threats (Greenland, the Panama Canal, Gaza, Ukraine) are a cohesive assault that is destroying that expectation. The remedy is for midsize and small states, the General Assembly and new coalitions to share enforcement, while admitting the old system's flaws.

READING 2 · ARGUMENT · PP. 140–168

A Racialized Existence

Dimitrios A. Kourtis, “A Racialized Existence: Lessons from Palestine and the Genocide Convention”, ch. 7 in Mohsen al Attar and Claire Smith (eds), Emancipating International Law (Oxford University Press, 2026), pp. 140–168.

The Genocide Convention protects “racial groups”, but existing readings of race (visible traits, the perpetrator's view, or the 1940s meaning) all fail. Kourtis argues race is a dynamic, relational social construct produced by a “racial contract” that law itself mediates, so a racial group is one whose identity is “hybrid, situational, fragmentary, and negotiable”. Applying this to Palestinians, from the Mandate to Israeli citizenship, land and security law, he argues that their racialization, which he calls tantamount to apartheid, “primed” genocide, and that after 7 October 2023 the conditions were “activated”. Palestinians therefore qualify as a protected group.

READING 1 · FOREIGN AFFAIRS, JULY/AUGUST 2025

Might Unmakes Right

Hathaway is Professor of Law at Yale Law School, a Nonresident Scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and President-elect of the American Society of International Law. Shapiro is Professor of Law at Yale Law School and Professor of Philosophy at Yale. They wrote The Internationalists: How a Radical Plan to Outlaw War Remade the World.

Opening: a cohesive assault

pp. 80–82

In his first months back in office, US President Donald Trump:

  • threatened to use military force to seize Greenland and the Panama Canal;
  • suggested the US could take ownership of Gaza after the expulsion of two million Palestinians;
  • demanded that Ukraine give up territory to Russia in exchange for a cease-fire.
Hathaway & Shapiro

These are not just typical, hyperbolic bluster. They are “a cohesive assault on a long-standing principle of international law: that states are prohibited from threatening or using military force against other states to resolve disputes” (pp. 80–81).

How the prohibition was built

Before the twentieth century, legal theorists believed not only that countries could wage war to seize land and resources but that in some circumstances they should. War was legal: the primary way to enforce national rights and resolve disputes. That changed in 1928, when nearly every country joined the Kellogg–Briand Pact, agreeing that wars of aggression should be illegal and conquest prohibited. The 1945 UN Charter reaffirmed and expanded this, putting at its core a prohibition on the “threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state”. Having found that agreeing to prohibit war was not enough, states built frameworks and institutions to cement the rule: a new legal order that elevated economic tools over military might.

What it achieved

  • Wars between states became far less common. In the 65 years after the last settlements of the Second World War, the territory conquered each year fell to less than six percent of what it had been for just over a century before war was outlawed.
  • The number of countries tripled from 1945 to today, as states stopped fearing being “gobbled up” by powerful neighbours.
  • Countries traded more freely, knowing their wealth was less likely to be plundered. The world became more peaceful and prosperous.

Erosion, then collapse

The prohibition's influence had eroded before Trump returned: the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, justified by weapons of mass destruction Iraq did not possess; China's decade of building military bases in contested areas of the South China Sea; Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the largest land war in Europe since 1945. “But Trump is shredding what is left of the norm against using force.” (p. 81)

Until now the US played a critical, if imperfect, role in defending the post-war order. That order's resilience depended less on total compliance than on a shared set of expectations: even a state not committed to the prohibition knew that violating it would likely bring condemnation, sanctions and perhaps lawful intervention by the US and its allies. “Now, that expectation is gone.” Trump is not merely abandoning the US role; he seems to want to restore war, or the threat of it, as the main way states resolve disagreements and seek economic gain.

Other states are already signalling that the norms have changed:

  • Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appeared to endorse Trump's musings about Gaza.
  • Panama placated Trump by accepting deportation flights of non-Panamanians and signing an agreement letting US military personnel deploy along the Canal.
  • Amid Trump's threats to let Putin annex parts of Ukraine, Kyiv signed a deal giving the US access to its mineral resources.
Hathaway & Shapiro

If left unchecked, the erosion will return geopolitics to “a raw contest of military power”. The consequences: a global arms race, renewed wars of conquest, shrinking trade, and the collapse of the cooperation needed to confront shared global threats (p. 82).

Entrenched warfare

pp. 82–84 · the old order, when war was law

For centuries before the First World War, war was a legally recognised way of resolving disputes. “The outbreak of war did not constitute a breakdown of the international order—it was the order.” With no global court, sovereigns enforced their rights by going to war, setting out their legal reasoning in war manifestos. Any legal grievance could be a just cause: damage to property such as ships, unpaid debts, treaty violations, and self-defence. Hugo Grotius, “the father of international law”, wrote in Commentary on the Law of Prize and Booty that a “war is said to be ‘just’ if it consists in the execution of a right”.

The right of conquest

Because war enforced rights, international law recognised a right of conquest: land and property could be seized to remedy the wrong. Grotius: states attain “through war that which is rightfully [theirs]”. Powers often took what was not rightfully theirs, but with no supreme authority to judge, the system effectively presumed every conquest just. “Might made right.”

  1. 1846The US war against Mexico, justified mainly by Mexico's unpaid debts. Mexico was forced to cede 525,000 square miles (the future American Southwest) for $15 million and the cancellation of its debts.
  2. 1854Gunboat diplomacy (military threats to win political or economic demands, often through unequal treaties): Commodore Matthew Perry sailed warships into Edo (Tokyo) Bay, claiming a legal right to trade and threatening force. On 31 March 1854 the Treaty of Kanagawa opened two Japanese ports to US ships. If waging war for rights was justified, so was threatening it.
  3. 1814–15War was law enforcement, not a crime. After losing the War of the Sixth Coalition, Napoleon was sent to Elba, keeping the title of emperor and ruling the island as a sovereign. His later exile to St Helena after Waterloo was a preventive quarantine, not punishment.

Neutrality

Neutral states owed strict duties of impartiality: they could not sanction warring parties, since that interfered with belligerents asserting their rights, and breaching neutrality was itself a just cause for war. “Conquest was lawful, but imposing economic sanctions against belligerents was not.” (p. 84)

Hathaway & Shapiro

Under this order, which lasted into the early twentieth century, powerful states freely resorted to war and weaker ones submitted or risked annihilation: “a near-constant churn of conflict”. Borders shifted through violence, empires expanded by force and entrenched global inequalities, trade routes were opened and controlled with cannons, colonial possessions were “won and lost like damages in a lawsuit”, and the world economy was stunted by the constant threat of war.

From war to peace

pp. 84–88 · outlawing war, and what it built

  1. 1914–18The First World War brought destructive new technologies to the battlefield, and its devastation far outstripped earlier wars: more than 20 countries fought, and an estimated 20 million died, about half of them civilians. Once the killing stopped, “a desperate search began” for a way to prevent another such catastrophe.
  2. 1920The League of Nations was founded for collective security, but the US Senate blocked US membership, hobbling its enforcement power.
  3. 1927–28US Secretary of State Frank Kellogg proposed a treaty to French Prime Minister Aristide Briand. Within a year the Kellogg–Briand Pact (the General Treaty for Renunciation of War as an Instrument of National Policy) had 58 signatories. Parties agreed to “condemn recourse to war for the solution of international controversies, and renounce it, as an instrument of national policy in their relations with one another”, and to settle disputes “by pacific means”.
  4. 1931–32Japan invaded Manchuria. Secretary of State Henry Stimson took a year to craft a response: the US would refuse to recognise Japan's right to illegally seized land, and League members followed. This Stimson Doctrine of nonrecognition was a turning point: conquest would no longer be recognised, nor would a coerced treaty transferring the land. “Gunboat diplomacy would no longer give rise to valid treaty obligations.”
  5. 1939–46Germany and Japan, both parties to the Pact, flouted it but lost all their conquests, and their leaders were tried. The first count at Nuremberg charged that “the aggressive war prepared by the Nazi conspirators ... had been specifically planned in advance, in violation of the terms of the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928”.
  6. 1941US Attorney General Robert Jackson defended the Lend-Lease Act (arming states fighting Nazi Germany without declaring war) because the Pact had changed neutrality: “the state which has gone to war in violation of its obligations acquires no right to equality of treatment from other states”.
  7. 1945The UN Charter codified the revolution: states are prohibited from “the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state”. Treaties signed under coercion became formally void, neutrality no longer required impartiality, and aggressors could be held criminally responsible.
Hathaway & Shapiro

The Pact is “widely mocked as naive and ineffective” because it failed to prevent the Second World War, but it set in motion the process that produced the modern international legal order. Its authors failed to appreciate the scale of what they had done: once war was outlawed, nearly every part of international law had to be reimagined. “Norms, in other words, began shifting in 1928”, but ideals needed legal rules and institutions to give them force. The shift, led by the US, was “one of the most profound legal transformations in world history” (p. 86).

The evidence of the peace

  • Great powers have not openly fought each other since 1945, and no UN member state has permanently ceased to exist through conquest.
  • The century before the Second World War saw over 150 successful territorial conquests; the decades since, fewer than ten.
  • Rival explanations (nuclear deterrence, the spread of democracy, global trade) “fail to account for the importance of the decision to outlaw war”.
  • Kuwait, 1990: when Saddam Hussein invaded in August 1990, the Security Council demanded withdrawal, then authorised states to “use all necessary means” to “restore international peace and security”, and a US-led coalition expelled Iraq. States learned that violations have consequences.
Hathaway & Shapiro: how the law works

“The law shaped states' behavior not necessarily because they decided that they ought to follow it. It shaped their behavior because it changed how they expected other states—especially the United States—to respond.” (p. 87)

From conquest to trade, from gunboats to checkbooks

  • Before, wealth depended on how much territory, resources and concessions a state could capture; war and conquest were recognised paths to prosperity. Eliminating conquest forced states to grow peacefully, mainly through trade. Trade expansion and the prohibition of war went hand in hand: economic cooperation, market competition, and the free flow of goods and capital.
  • Great powers swapped gunboat diplomacy for checkbook diplomacy. Economic and diplomatic sanctions replaced war as the primary way to enforce international law. States designed ways of outcasting: excluding violators from the benefits of cooperation, for example through trade sanctions for human rights violations, supporting terrorism or aggressive war.
  • Interdependence grew: trade was about 10% of world GDP in 1945 and 58% by 2023; tens of thousands of international organisations and more than 250,000 treaties emerged. Exclusion became harder and harder to bear.

The US as enforcer: imperfect but functional

With its huge share of global GDP and the dollar as reserve currency, the US gained extraordinary power to enforce the rules; staying on good terms with it was a financial imperative. Its record was far from perfect: Vietnam, the 2003 invasion of Iraq and its multidecade counterterrorism campaign in the Middle East all rested on overly broad claims of self-defence. But it never violated the essential prohibition on territorial conquest, and it upheld the system: pledging to defend NATO's European members, the American states of the Rio Treaty, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, the Philippines, South Korea and Thailand, and leading the response to Iraq's invasion of Kuwait even without a treaty obligation. This “imperfect but functional system” kept major conflicts at bay and let states prosper without fearing conquest or unequal treaties.

Legal jeopardy

pp. 88–90 · what Trump is doing to the order

Hathaway & Shapiro

“Prior U.S. administrations can be condemned for their hypocrisy.” But the Trump administration's willingness to give up the prohibition altogether is “far more dangerous”. The idea that the US could acquire Canada, Greenland or the Panama Canal by force, or claim Gaza, “is not mere realism or a new form of transactional politics based on dealmaking. It is a throwback to an earlier era when might made right.” It revives the pre-Kellogg–Briand idea that threatening war or conquest is a legitimate way to force concessions (pp. 88–89).

The attack has several fronts:

  • Abandoning others' right not to be conquered. In April, after threatening to pull military aid, Trump warned President Zelensky that if he would not consider a US-brokered peace plan, which according to the Financial Times could cede 20 percent of Ukraine's territory to Russia, he would face “losing [his] whole country”.
  • Reviving gunboat diplomacy. Military threats helped extract concessions from Canada and Mexico.
  • Blunting sanctions. Sanctions work best when used rarely and against clear violations. Slapping 25 percent tariffs on Canada and Mexico “on a whim” corrodes their force as punishment for real unlawful behaviour.
  • Turning sanctions against the law. An executive order threatening sanctions on judges and lawyers associated with the International Criminal Court “turned a tool for enforcing international law into a weapon to undermine it”.
  • Unravelling interdependence. Isolationist economic policies weaken other states' ability to punish breaches by outcasting, leaving them the choice of military force or unchecked violations.
Hathaway & Shapiro

The chaos is a wider attempt to dismantle the post-war legal order, and it is especially dangerous because it comes from the country that built and maintained that system. Courts, domestic opposition, or other leaders' reluctance may block some threats, but the threats alone erode the assumptions (about behaviour, restraint and consequences) that uphold the prohibition. Those assumptions let weaker states plan for the long term, investors commit capital across borders and governments respond collectively to violations. If the most powerful state flouts them with impunity, others will too, and the system will crumble “not all at once, but piece by piece until it collapses altogether” (p. 90).

The right fight

pp. 90–93 · what should be done

If the prohibition collapses

Putin, Trump and Xi Jinping may carve the world into spheres of influence, each free to terrorise the states in its sphere and extract concessions for protection. Such a world might be quiescent for a while but would be far less free. More likely, incessant conflict returns: the world of Thucydides, where “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must”.

The other path

  • Reaffirm the prohibition without the US as chief enforcer. In 2022, 142 countries joined the US in a General Assembly resolution condemning Russia's attempted annexation of Ukrainian territory as unlawful.
  • Europe is stepping in. After the “disastrous” March White House meeting in which Trump and Vice President JD Vance belittled Zelensky, Europe rallied: UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer pledged more European military spending and a “coalition of the willing”, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised an EU support plan.
Hathaway & Shapiro

But Europe cannot replace the US as the world's policeman: it lacks the military power, economic influence and political unity, and relying heavily on another single actor would be a mistake anyway. Any serious defence of the prohibition must acknowledge the problems with the system that secured it:

  • the five permanent members (China, France, the Soviet Union, the UK, the US) gave themselves a veto over any UN enforcement;
  • US dominance meant that when Washington broke the rules, as in Iraq in 2003, “nobody was able to hold it to account”.

These flaws delegitimised the order, especially in the eyes of the global South, so some states may not value what they stand to lose. Publicly acknowledging the order's weaknesses, and its defenders' failures to live up to their own ideals, is the first step. A renewed system must empower a wider variety of states to share responsibility for upholding the norms, making them more legitimate and resilient to political shifts in any one country (p. 91).

Their proposals

  1. Broad coalitions of midsize and small states. Analysts assume peace needs a single powerful guarantor, but underestimate the power of states working together. The EU shows it: none of its 27 members is a great power alone, but together they are a force.
  2. A stronger General Assembly. All 193 members have an equal vote. It lacks the Security Council's enforcement powers, but as an organ responsible for peace and security it can assert more power. The “veto initiative”, created after Russia invaded Ukraine, sends any vetoed Security Council resolution to the Assembly for debate. Resolutions under it gave states legal backing to coordinate sanctions on Russia and arm and fund Ukraine, and led to an international register of damages for postwar reparations.
  3. Regional and issue-specific coalitions. The Council of Europe is setting up a court to gather evidence against Putin and other Russian leaders and eventually try them for the crime of aggression. The Hague Group (Bolivia, Colombia, Cuba, Honduras, Malaysia, Namibia, Senegal and South Africa) is working to enforce ICJ and ICC decisions on the war in Gaza. In May, African Union and EU foreign ministers pledged a stronger partnership on peace and security, a possible starting point for a peace coalition that does not rely on the US.
  4. An “outcasting council”. Only the Security Council can authorise force to enforce the law, but nothing stops states creating an organisation to authorise joint sanctions against violators of the prohibition and other critical laws. Ad hoc sanctions are slow and unpredictable; automatic, coordinated responses would work far better.

Making the US pay, and the risks

Above all, states must recognise how much good the prohibition has enabled, how hard it was to establish, and how much chaos would follow its loss. If they replace the US enforcement role with new institutions, that sends a powerful signal: American leaders who claim might makes right would be in the minority and isolated. If Washington tried to seize the Panama Canal, for example, states could outcast the US with sanctions and diplomatic penalties, or by withdrawing permission for US bases. Showing that states can jointly impose costs on the US would counter Trump's damage and affirm that a wider variety of countries can play “a more equal role in shaping and enforcing international law” (p. 93).

  • Trump is not the only threat: China and Russia are also trying to reshape norms, but broad collective enforcement would make them take notice too.
  • It is unclear whether France, Germany and the UK, used to dictating the terms, will share power, or whether countries long excluded will trust an order grounded in the prohibition.
  • Developing countries may gain in the short term by playing China, Russia and the US off against each other, but in the long run they risk “becoming the spoils of great-power rivalries, with little capacity to direct or control their own futures”.
Hathaway & Shapiro: the close

The system “is not self-sustaining. It must be vigorously defended.” After the Second World War broke out, US policymakers saw that failing to build a durable order after the First had sown chaos; waiting for a crisis to pass before planning is “a recipe for failure”. Like the policymakers of the 1940s, today's leaders must “design institutions, alliances, and strategies to secure peace rather than sit and watch as Trump rewinds the clock” (p. 93).

READING 2 · EMANCIPATING INTERNATIONAL LAW (OUP, 2026), CH. 7

A Racialized Existence

A legal-theoretical and socio-legal argument about the meaning of “racial groups” in the Genocide Convention, applied to Palestinians. The chapter makes strong, contested claims (apartheid, genocidal priming and activation). Everything below reports Kourtis's argument in his own terms.

1. Introduction

pp. 140–142

Genocide is “a powerful word” and a highly contested legal concept. More than seventy years after the term emerged and shaped the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide adopted 9 Dec 1948 · in force 12 Jan 1951, relatively little attention has gone to the protected groups, which are the ultimate victims of the crime and the right-holders of the underlying primary right of existence. Two questions are open:

  • whether the four protected groups (national, ethnic, racial and religious) should be read subjectively or objectively;
  • how each of this “protected tetrad” is to be defined, and whether they form one broad category or several interconnected ones.

fn The right to exist is grounded in GA Res 96(I) (1946) and the case law: Bosnia v Serbia (ICJ 2007), Croatia v Serbia (ICJ 2015), The Gambia v Myanmar (provisional measures, 2020), South Africa v Israel (provisional measures, 2024), Akayesu (ICTR 1998) and Krstić (ICTY 2001).

Race is the hardest case. Article II prohibits genocide against, among others, racial groups, yet protecting a group defined by race in the “crime of crimes” fn the ICTR's phrase in Kambanda (1998) seems to defy international criminal law's preference for objectivity. Race is widely regarded as a discredited category in science, so it may seem odd or dangerous to use it to define a protected group. Racial groups appear in the definitions of genocide and of crimes against humanity (apartheid and persecution), but few scholars offer a framework for an idea that (in Schabas's words) “has become virtually obsolete”. Most existing interpretations are subjectivist and perpetrator-based, which gives little clarity on how a group racialized arbitrarily by perpetrators can claim the right to exist.

Kourtis: the hypothesis

Including racial groups carries a distinct normative message: the four ascriptive collectivities are more than permanent, stable or inescapable. “They are dynamic and relational social constructs conferring a collective identity with strong links to both in-group and out-group perceptions.” (p. 141)

The idea that racialized realities can trigger the Convention's protection is not new. In Akayesu ICTR 1998 the Rwanda tribunal labelled the Tutsi a permanent and stable group, protected by an ejusdem generis reading of its Statute's Article 2, without classifying them as ethnic or racial. Even so, it conceded that everyone, including their killers, considered the Tutsi a distinct ethnic group. Kourtis adds a standalone analysis of racial groups as a protected category, and of what protection means for a racial (or racialized) collective facing collective violence.

Roadmap: how racial groups were conceived in drafting and interpreted afterwards; an alternative reading drawing on social science about racialization and collective identity; its application to Palestinians as racialized subjects; the link to an evolving “atrocity spectrum”, using the criminology and victimology of genocide; and closing remarks on the debate over calling events in Gaza genocide.

Kourtis: the claim in full

Race, though ambiguously defined in the drafting, remains pivotal for identifying genocidal conditions. Racialized collective identities are built through universal and localized racial contracts that legitimize and normalize systemic oppression, dispossession and violence, and through them the individual and collective racialized subject emerges. That subject, though the product of subjugation, is the primary holder of the collective right of existence that the Convention guarantees through prevention and punishment. Its forming processes (oppression, domination, exclusion) are also the actus reus and mens rea of distinct crimes such as apartheid and persecution (p. 142).

Caveat: the chapter does not examine the apartheid regime which, it states, Israeli authorities established and perpetuate against Palestinians. It acknowledges a system of racialized oppression and domination and aims to complement apartheid analyses with “a long overdue discussion focused on genocide”.

2. The multiple meanings of race: from the Genocide Convention to post-1948 international law

pp. 143–149

Race, racism and genocide

The link is well established. Tawia Ansah argues the concept of genocide was created by drawing a line between civilized warfare and barbarous (racial) “blood wars”, and Dirk Moses shows persecution on racial grounds was decisive in its early formation. Kourtis argues the link runs deeper:

  • Lemkin. Raphael Lemkin, who coined the word, derived it from the Greek genos, meaning “race” or “tribe”, and presented genocide as Nazi Germany's racial masterplan, a way to win all wars through the “vantage point” of racial superiority. His idea of race was distinctly cultural, even ethnonational, but early on also biopolitical (blood and peoplehood); citing the Nazi ideologue Alfred Rosenberg, he called Germany's new world order a plan of racial domination. This ambiguous idea set the new crime apart from earlier interwar debates (the failed anti-terrorism convention, the minorities treaties) and tied it to the image of German aggression as a racial order imposed on Europe's “captive nations”. So race “de-politicized and essentialized the debate on Nazi criminality”.
  • Article II. Including racial groups met practically no resistance, because it fitted prevailing ideas of permanence, stability and inescapability. The drafters used the same ideas to exclude more variable groups: political groups, liberation movements, and peoples under colonial domination.
  • The World Jewish Congress. In the late 1940s its communications to ECOSOC warned of “extreme and imminent danger” to Jewish communities in the Middle East, a “racial and religious group whose human rights and fundamental freedoms are being violated”. They protested Arab resistance to the 1947 Partition Plan as a “declaration of war” and a “peril of annihilation”, and amounted to genocide and discrimination claims against Arab states. Kourtis reads the strategy as using genocide “as an antidote to the extreme politicization” of Palestine while the Zionist leadership fought to establish the state, with its representative insisting the question was separate from Palestine's political future. “Allegations of racism and genocide quickly emerged, if only to conceal the true political and colonial character of the conflict.”

These encounters show the tangled relationship between the apex crime and political struggles. Although Article II protected racial groups, neither the drafters nor the UN would accept that systemic violence grounded in racialized oppression, domination and dispossession could be called genocide. fn For example the fate of the Civil Rights Congress's 1951 petition against the US, We Charge Genocide. Still, protecting racial groups became the chapeau of the norm codifying genocide.

What the drafters meant by “racial”

The constituent elements of a racial group got little attention. Racial groups appeared in every draft, including the original Cuba–India–Panama proposal and General Assembly Resolution 96(I), but were never analysed. The records mostly show objections to adding “ethnical” because it seemed identical to “racial”. The travaux give no single answer:

  • Biological readings. Norway and Haiti thought racial and ethnic groups could be distinguished biologically. Haiti: “intermingling between races in certain regions has made the problem of race so complicated that it might be impossible, in certain cases, to consider a given group as a racial group, although it could not be denied classification as an ethnical group”. Sweden distinguished race from traditions and cultural heritage. Race was treated as immutable, a matter of fortune: the UK said “[n]o one should be persecuted because of the accident of his birth”.
  • National and ethnic readings. Egypt saw “no great difference” between racial and ethnic groups. China, Czechoslovakia and Mexico called their own peoples “races”. The UK invoked “the six million human beings [that] had been coldly and deliberately exterminated with a view to destroying the Jewish race”. Belgium saw “racial” and “ethnical” as identical, citing the minorities treaties. Iran treated “racial” and “national” as equivalent, their “distinctive features were permanent”. The Netherlands put race and nationality on an equal footing, and the Soviet delegate saw them as cognates forming “distinct, clearly determinable communities”.
  • The term carried “a colossal ideological burden”, given the recent racial persecution and genocide and European racial violence against colonized peoples, yet post-war jurisprudence (the Nuremberg judgment) and the framers endorsed it.

The minorities treaties. In the interwar period nobody seriously argued that racial groups were biologically distinct. Anthony Eden said the minorities problem “is not the existence of different races or religions within one country, but the fact that a minority in one country is adjacent to a majority of its own race, language or religion in a neighbouring country”, and European Jews were described as “a race scattered through all countries”. So “racial” was probably premised on cultural nationality or ethnicity. The framers' practice supports this: in 1948 Greece accused its communist neighbours and its own nationals of plotting to “destroy the Greek race”; in 1950 US Deputy Under-Secretary Dean Rusk told the Senate the Holocaust was the “organized butchery of racial groups”; similar language was used in the House of Commons. So race as ethnonational identity was not discredited during the drafting.

The tautology

Genocide was first conceived as a crime of motive, and motive was essential. The Lebanese delegate noted there was “nothing to correspond to the racial hatred or religious fanaticism which usually motivated acts of genocide” in ordinary crime. Motive gave the crime its collective dimension, one collectivity targeting another, making it a “collective crime” or “crime sui generis”, with race as the reason a group was slated for annihilation. The motive element was later dropped, but a tautology survived: race defined the racial group, and the racial group was defined by race. That made members “defenceless” because their condition was “inevitable”, a way to target “human beings whom chance alone had grouped together”.

After 1948: biology never quite left

  • Early commentators such as Antonio Planzer oscillated between biological and cultural readings.
  • India told the ICJ (in the Right of Passage pleadings) that “[t]he people of Dadra and Nagar Aveli are of Indian race, the great majority being Hindus, speaking the same language as the inhabitants of the surrounding Indian territory”.
  • Judge Tanaka in South West Africa ICJ 1966: “as a matter of common-sense [the] criteria to distinguish one race from the other, are the appearance, particularly physical characteristics such as colour, hair, etc”.
  • The European Court of Human Rights in Timishev v Russia 2005: “the notion of race is rooted in the idea of biological classification of human beings into subspecies according to morphological features such as skin colour or facial characteristics”.

Human rights law defines race differently

There is little practice defining racial groups under the Convention or the Rome Statute, in contrast to human rights and anti-discrimination law:

  • ICERD 1965 · art. 1(1) defines racial discrimination as “any distinction, exclusion, restriction or preference based on race, colour, descent, or national or ethnic origin”. Its Committee (CERD) treats membership of racial or ethnic groups as primarily self-identification.
  • Egon Schwelb: racial discrimination is broader than race (covering colour, descent, national and ethnic origin). Michael Banton (a former CERD member): race is the outcome of subjective ascriptions and socially constructed realities, with the discriminator's ascriptions prevailing.
  • Like science, human rights law treats biological race as a falsity tied to racist ideology fn UNESCO statements on race of 1950, 1967 and 1978, whereas genocide law treats race as a characteristic that ascribes an identity needing protection.
Kourtis

Human rights law aims to stigmatize and tackle discrimination on grounds of race; the Convention aims to protect the physical existence of groups defined by such grounds. “In human rights law discourse, race is the by-product of discrimination, whereas, in the law against genocide, it is the reason for recognizing the group's collective right to exist and be free from annihilating violence.” The two bodies of law serve different purposes and may define race differently (p. 148).

Apartheid law differs again. In apartheid, a crime against humanity, the key is the domination of one racial group over another within institutionalized oppression, so the oppressed group's racial identity is shaped by the very system the crime presupposes. Focusing on South Africa, as the 1973 Apartheid Convention does, racial groups must be read in the broadest social sense, with the oppressors' perceptions prevailing. These divergent meanings show the aporia (the unresolved puzzle) of interpreting Article II.

Three trends in international criminal law

  1. Objective / visible traits. Following the US Proxmire Act 18 USC §1093(6) and Akayesu: race means externally visible hereditary characteristics, usually with some bond among members beyond the traits, though this “togetherness” is looser than in other groups.
  2. Subjective / perpetrator. Race exists only in the perpetrators' ascriptions (Lingaas, Fournet).
  3. Historical. Led by William Schabas: race should be read as the framers understood it in the 1940s; otherwise the Convention's protective scope shrinks and the drafters' aim of the broadest protection is defeated.

3. A critique of the existing interpretations

pp. 149–151

  • The first reading sees racial groups as biological “visible minorities” with only light solidarity.
  • The second cuts the Gordian knot by denying the group any trans-subjective existence, locating it in the perpetrators' minds.
  • The third, Schabas's holistic “four corner posts” approach, merges race into a larger whole resembling the interwar concept of minorities, and by reading race in its early-twentieth-century sense avoids dealing with a notion bound up with racism: in the 1940s the logic of race “was still valid, at least to some”.

Why each fails

  • Visible minority. It follows everyday meaning and case law, but cannot explain how pigmentation creates solidarity without any other bond.
  • Pure subjectivism. Its appeal ends once the right to exist is at stake. “Right-holders cannot be hypothesized.” They either exist in a trans-subjective, socially verified way, or they are aggregates of victimized individuals whose rights arise only once violated (p. 150).
  • Schabas's historical reading has the most historical merit (race was less monolithic in the 1940s, and the drafters disagreed on biology versus culture while insisting on inclusion), but it rests on three assumptions:
    1. Primo: that the referent was meant to stay fixed. “Racial group” is a generic referencing expression for a class of phenomena, not a specific group such as the Ottoman Armenians, and can have an alterable referent. The Convention's object and purpose, and the drafters' decision to omit references to fascism, Nazism, Nuremberg and crimes against humanity, suggest referents were not assumed fixed.
    2. Secundo: that all delegates understood race the same way. Sweden and Haiti leaned biological; Egypt, Uruguay and Belgium leaned sociocultural.
    3. Tertio: that ordinary meaning is frozen at the time of drafting. That linguistic anachronism clashes with interpretation principles: a term is read “within the framework of the entire legal system prevailing at the time of interpretation” (Namibia advisory opinion, 1971), presuming the drafters meant to “follow the evolution of the law” (Aegean Sea, 1978), especially for long-lived treaties.

where the parties have used generic terms in a treaty, the parties necessarily having been aware that the meaning of the terms was likely to evolve over time, and where the treaty has been entered into for a very long period or is ‘of continuing duration’, the parties must be presumed, as a general rule, to have intended those terms to have an evolving meaning.

Costa Rica v Nicaragua (ICJ 2009), quoted at p. 151
Kourtis

Race is a temporal and dynamic concept, so it must be read from today's perspective, in contemporary usage. The same rule applies to the other groups: the drafters hardly meant to exclude religious groups that emerged after 1948 by “freezing” the meaning (p. 151).

4. The racialized subject

pp. 151–160

A synthesis of the three readings

Each approach captures something: the historical reading insists on everyday meaning even though race is scientifically discredited; the subjectivist one shows racial groups are products of ascription with no immutable existence outside their social context; the visible-minority one identifies the anchor points of ascription, arbitrarily chosen external traits seen as hereditary, which others use to ascribe identity and the group uses to self-identify.

So race implies visibility and interaction. It is not a natural given but a “normative phantasm” (Judith Butler): a set of identification practices attached to the racialized subject regardless of its true nature and agency.

The racial contract

The racialized subject is the normative product of what Charles Mills called the racial contract: a heuristic for the “set of formal or informal agreements or meta-agreements” among a group designated racially superior, against others debased as inferior. It is political, moral and epistemological, but also highly juridified, mediated by domestic and international legal institutions. The contract is global, but localized contracts also exist, especially on the fringes of the dominant group's space; the Mediterranean, the Balkans and the Middle East show the limits of the global contract, where it operates in modified form.

Palestine: the contract in international law

  • Colonial foundations. The contract's foundations lie in colonialism and European domination of the Orient, including the League of Nations mandates system (Noura Erakat).
  • Erasure in text. The 1917 Balfour Declaration and the 1922 Mandate for Palestine linguistically erased the Arab Palestinian community, calling Palestinians “existing non-Jewish communities” or “sections of the population”. Kourtis: thus “the preamble of the racial contract between a community that was not present in the territory but sought to claim it and one that was there but was subject to textual elision and political silencing was sanctioned and institutionalized in international law by dint of the Mandate” (p. 152).
  • UNSCOP and partition. The 1947 report of the UN Special Committee on Palestine justified denying the Indigenous community's self-determination by citing the “antagonistic” Jewish national claim and the Jewish “National Home”, casting Palestine as a conflict in which one group had to be suppressed for the other to prosper. The Partition Plan GA Res 181(II), 29 Nov 1947 was likewise “a process of erasure” that ignored the obligations of the Mandatory Power and international authority and institutionalized inequalities. UNSCOP's idealized two-state Palestine assigned each community “national” characteristics to flourish under a supposedly impartial international authority, but this “idealized racial Palestine was destined to remain a contingency story of international law”.

The contract in Israeli law

Kourtis argues the establishment of Israel was accompanied by persecution, uprooting and ethnic cleansing of Arab Palestinians (citing Pappé) and by laws solidifying the localized contract:

  • Declaration of Independence (14 May 1948). It promised “full social and political equality of all its citizens, without distinction of race, creed or sex”, but founded a state as a Jewish National Home open to anyone of Jewish heritage, a political community bound by ethnic, spiritual and even racial allegiance. Citizenship became a narrative of belonging, producing uneven citizenship. The Israeli Supreme Court held in 1972 and 2013 (Ornan v Ministry of the Interior) that the only nationality recognised is Jewish, so there is no Israeli nationality separate from Jewish identity. fn Jewish identity itself has a complex relationship with race.
  • Law of Return (1950) and Citizenship Law (1952). Every oleh (Jewish immigrant) is entitled to citizenship. Of four paths (return, residence, birth, naturalization), “return” is limited to people of Jewish heritage, while “residence” requires Palestinians to prove residence before 1948, registration and continuous presence or lawful entry between 1948 and 1952. Those uprooted in the 1940s or left off the registry remain “citizen strangers” (Shira Robinson).
  • Basic Law: Israel – The Nation State of the Jewish People (2018). It “constitutionalizes the condition of non-belonging as the quintessence of the racial contract”: Israel is the national home of the Jewish people, who are the sole bearers of self-determination; Jerusalem, “united and complete”, is the capital; the ingathering of exiles gains constitutional status; and settlements, which are illegal under international law (Wall advisory opinion, 2004), receive preferential treatment. A 2020 Israeli court (Nezar Bakri v Karmiel Municipality) held Jewish settlement “a national value ... and a worthy and dominant consideration” in administrative decisions.
  • Absentees' Property Law (1950), “the flagship” of permanent dispossession, covering refugees and internally displaced people. Land could be confiscated into state custody if its owner (i) was a citizen or national of specified enemy countries, (ii) was in hostile countries or parts of Palestine outside Israel's control, (iii) left Palestine before September 1948, or (iv) moved to areas held by forces opposing the state. The period ran from 29 November 1947 to the end of the state of emergency. Amendments created “present-absentees” (internally displaced Palestinians, some living near their former property). Property passed to state and quasi-state bodies for the benefit of Jewish nationals, and after 1967 occupation brought further appropriation, eviction and confiscation over five decades.
Kourtis

“Land seizure, denial of entry, and de facto denationalization thus constitute the essence of the Palestinian racialized subject.” (p. 155)

Security, surveillance and the “law of the enemy”

  • The identity is further shaped by portraying Palestinians as “state enemies”, by emergency regulations in force since 1948, and by biopolitical control and surveillance: control of movement and communications, barriers, the Wall, checkpoints and permits.
  • Israeli law towards Palestinians is a form of the “law of the enemy”, producing what David Theo Goldberg calls racial Palestinianization: denial of agency, and the image of Palestinians as suspect by definition, ontologically threatening and perennially foreign.
  • Israel's Penal Law 1977 · art. 91 defines an enemy very broadly: “anyone who is a belligerent, maintains a state of war against Israel or declares himself one of those, whether or not a war was declared ... and [is] also a [member of a] terrorist organisation”. Interactions with “enemy” collectivities are penalized.
  • Since 2003, special provisions have effectively barred family reunification between Israeli citizens and Palestinian spouses fn latest version: Citizenship and Entry into Israel Law (Temporary Order), 2022, based on belonging to the Palestinian communities of “the areas”, not on individual security assessment. Kourtis says this “further evinces an apartheid system”.

How racialization shapes self-identity

  • The multilayered identity was forged through persecution, ethnic cleansing, displacement, and precarious life in diaspora, in refugee camps, or within the territories.
  • The Palestinian National Covenant (1968) defines Palestinian identity as “a genuine, essential, and inherent characteristic” that “is transmitted from parents to children”.
  • A 2007 Palestinian election decree disenfranchises Palestinians who acquired Israeli citizenship, so Israeli “citizen” status (even nominal) excludes them from the Palestinian body politic. fn Israel follows the same rule: a 2008 amendment on revoking citizenship.

Law mediates the identity

  • Refugees' tripartite right to return, restitution and/or compensation, set out in GA Resolution 194(III) 11 Dec 1948, one of the most reaffirmed resolutions and evidence of juridical consensus, is subordinated in Israeli law to raison d'état.
  • Under the Basic Law: Israel Lands (1960), appropriated land is res extra commercium: it cannot be bought or transferred to private people, including original owners, and stays with state agencies whose mandates discriminate against non-Jews.
  • Double standards: settlers live under civil law and Palestinians in the territories under military or emergency law, applied with wide discretion. The racialized subject is excluded from the “law of the friend” and debased by the “law of the enemy”: the Jewish legal subject is singular and uniform, the Palestinian one fragmented and conditional.

Kourtis calls this system of oppression and domination “tantamount to the crime of apartheid”.

Race as performative, situational, hybrid and negotiable

  • Performative. Racialized ascriptions “always have an agenda”, for example justifying dispossession as part of racial capitalism. Racialized subjectivity is a practice of both out-group and in-group that denotes what one is expected to do rather than what one is. The fixed idea of the Palestinian as terrorist, especially after the 1988 and 2000 uprisings, makes the subject a “de-civilianized security threat” whom police and even courts treat as such, sometimes pre-emptively. People growing up in the West Bank or Gaza internalize this (suspicion, fear, disobedience, outsmarting the system), producing W. E. B. Du Bois's double-consciousness: seeing oneself through the oppressor's eyes, even in the diaspora.
  • Situational. Racial definitions are about power as much as belonging. Mizrahi Jews (Jews of Arab descent) could be reconstituted as full subjects in post-1967 Israel because a racialized other emerged. Yehouda Shenhav on Arab-Jewish intelligence operatives of the 1950s–60s: “[b]y working for the state against the Arab enemy, [they] earned [their] entry ticket into Israeliness”.
  • Hybrid. A subject can deviate from the scripts: Article 7A, added in 2008 to the 1958 Basic Law: The Knesset, bars candidates who oppose “the existence of the state of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state” or who visited an “enemy country” unlawfully in the previous seven years. “Loyal” citizens are included only if they accept the state's non-negotiable Jewish identity, so, as John Reynolds observes, Palestinians are expected to legitimize the order that racializes them.
  • Negotiable. Israeli discourse distinguishes “good Arabs, who accept the Jewish rules of the game, and bad Arabs, who do not”. A 1996 study (Kaminsky and Bar-Tal) found “Arab Israelis” the least dehumanized label and “Palestinian supporters of the PLO” far more so, though the identities overlap. Subordination can be inversely proportional to compliance, and control extends to memory: a 2011 budget law amendment lets funding be withheld from bodies commemorating the Nakba, punishing remembrance and rewarding “forced forgetting”.
Kourtis: the definition

“A racial group constitutes a human figuration whose members are perceived and perceive themselves as having some different characteristics ascribing to them a distinct identity, the latter being hybrid, situational, fragmentary, and negotiable.” (p. 160)

5. A racialized existence: genocidal priming and activation

pp. 160–167

Not a new framing

  • During the drafting, Syria unsuccessfully proposed classifying as genocide measures “intended to oblige members of a group to abandon their homes in order to escape the [serious] threat of subsequent ill-treatment”.
  • About thirty years later, the General Assembly called the massacres of Palestinian refugees at Sabra and Shatila “genocide” GA Res 37/123D, 16 Dec 1982, its first post-1948 engagement with the concept, “fraught with symbolism, rhetorical accusations, and conflicting political motivations” (Cassese).

Rather than summarily applying the label, Kourtis examines how Palestinian racialization increases the risk of genocide.

The mechanics of othering

  • Genocide does not happen in a vacuum or spontaneously, and does not create identities from nothing. It makes a collective identity visible through dichotomization and stigmatization, then transforms it through extreme othering and dehumanization, drawing hard lines between dominant and subordinate groups.
  • Racialization does not demand genocide. The process is neither linear nor deterministic: there is room for de-escalation and a modus vivendi, and othering can instead end in encompassment (absorption, with cultural erasure short of physical destruction).
  • Alexander Hinton distinguishes essentializing othering (false dichotomies, identities seen as self-reproducing, as racialized identities are) from annihilating othering (cleansing the dominant group of an “alien” cast as an existential threat), which raises the risk of genocide and can consolidate the intent to destroy.
  • Othering often climaxes with a “trigger event” framed as an external or internal necessity, though its singularity is an illusion: it is a series of events moving the target group towards an existential threat that engages the Convention.

Priming

Genocidal priming is the coming together of factors that make genocide more likely in a given historical and sociopolitical context: situations become “hot” and volatile. Kourtis argues that the processes that constitute the racialized subject (racialization, marginalization, securitization, dehumanization) are also indispensable conditions of priming. Priming is dynamic, affected by domestic and international events, and can be “incremental” or “slow-boiling”, a series of escalating commitments that normalize the ideology and the violence. His candidates in the Israeli–Palestinian case: the Nakba and the establishment of Israel; phases of the conflict from the 1960s to the 1980s; the blockade of Gaza; and Operation Cast Lead (2008–09).

Activation

Priming is necessary but not sufficient, and may take decades: through each phase “the ‘heat’ increases” and the target group is brought “closer and closer to an existential precipice”. The risk materializes through genocidal activation: under extreme social control, leaders manipulate an event or series of events to present genocide as “a—if not ‘the’—rational choice”. “Architects” drive priming and activation through ideology, opportunity, communication and distortions of reality. An event framed as proof that the stigmatized group en bloc is an existential threat, with internal and external constraints absent or ineffective, can trigger activation even if it looks like a continuation of earlier violence. Activation can also build up through a chain of events over time. Because it needs impetus and organization, it happens only when the dominant group's leadership abandons normative and ethical constraints.

Kourtis's application: 7 October 2023

  • He traces such a decision to the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks (killings of soldiers, civilians and foreigners, rocket strikes, hostage-taking). The response was “yet another chapter in Israel's recourse to excessive force”, but he chooses it as the milestone of activation because of the relative “success” of prior priming and the existential rhetoric that followed.
  • The primers he lists: the “settler-colonialism mentality of Zionism”; Gaza's international isolation through occupation and apartheid; normalized disproportionate, selective and punitive force; regional and international realignments fostering impunity; and massive demographic changes over decades.
  • Rhetoric he cites: former Major General Giora Eiland calling the war existential; Minister Orit Strook calling a Palestinian state an “existential threat”; the Prime Minister framing a battle of civilization against barbarism; and judge ad hoc Aharon Barak, in opinions in the ICJ's provisional measures phase, describing an “existential threat” and a “second war of independence”. fn The footnote cites his dissenting opinion of 24 May 2024. For Kourtis, existential rhetoric even inside the ICJ shows October 2023 as the consummation of decades of priming.
  • Activation, he argues, required organization (a formation “bent on apartheid and violence”) and impetus (a presumed existential threat justifying the abrogation of constraints). He cites Defence Minister Yoav Gallant saying he “removed all restraints” on troop conduct, and Kjell Anderson's “humanity gap” for troops long trained in subjugation, now used for what he calls “Gaza's Nakba”.
  • After activation, Palestinians are stigmatized as existential threats, pariahs and “others in excess”; imagery such as “people of darkness” and “children of Amalek” normalizes dehumanization. These old tropes gain a new aetiology and purpose, justifying collective and indiscriminate destruction and turning racialization into an instrument of legitimization.

Apartheid as prelude

  • The 1973 Apartheid Convention (the International Convention on the Suppression and Punishment of the Crime of Apartheid) recognized that systems of racial domination could create conditions for a group's physical destruction.
  • Apartheid and genocide share structural features in their definitions, and South Africa's ICJ application set Israel's apartheid policies within a framework of genocidal acts in Gaza.
  • The transition turns on a shift in intent: apartheid's special intent is to sustain an oppressive regime; genocide's dolus specialis is to annihilate a group in whole or in part (Bosnia 2007, Croatia 2015, Gambia v Myanmar 2020). But apartheid can be a prelude, creating conditions in which the oppressed group is seen as expendable; Rwanda shows prolonged discrimination escalating into genocide.
  • In victimological terms, apartheid as a priming condition increased Palestinians' exposure to genocidal victimization, widened the “humanity gap”, and gave the leadership means to induce and justify violence. Edward Said: the thought that the other “is not quite as human as we” underlies oppression and may deny the other meaningful existence.

6. Conclusion

pp. 167–168

Kourtis

The Palestinians, as a racialized group, fit the criteria for protection under the Genocide Convention. The circumstances after 7 October 2023 and Operation Swords of Iron show conditions “alarmingly consistent with established genocidal processes”. The racial contract, perpetuated by domestic (Israeli) and international law, legitimized subjugation and the denial of agency and self-determination; it facilitated priming and activation by dehumanizing Palestinians and framing them as existential threats. Legitimized oppression, the impetus of the October attacks, and the apartheid power structure together allowed an escalation in which genocidal acts are “more readily justified and consummated” (pp. 167–168).

  • The abundance of Israeli officials' statements inciting and morally grounding the attacks “evince[s] a high probability of genocidal intent”.
  • In South Africa v Israel (formally, Application of the Genocide Convention in the Gaza Strip), the ICJ's provisional measures order 26 Jan 2024 used the leadership's statements when ruling on the plausibility of the rights and violations South Africa alleged.
  • Incitement matters because genocide is a collective endeavour: foot soldiers may or may not share the intent, but act within an atrocity context set by a power structure. So the Gaza context must be carefully documented. Stefan Kirsch: nuance can change a deed's meaning. A civilian killing in armed conflict does not look like genocide even with eliminatory intent, but the same killing amid genocidal incitement and propaganda calling on civilians to “take action” looks more suspect.

In the final analysis, there is some distance to be covered between subjugating and annihilating the racialized subject, and this distance can be bridged even by a single architect spiritus rector provided that ‘willing executioners’ are placed at their disposal.

The chapter's closing sentence, p. 168

How the week fits together

Connections

Two readings on the same post-1945 legal order, one defending its core prohibition, the other examining what its promises mean for a group the law has racialized.

Where they meet

  • The same order, two verdicts. Hathaway and Shapiro defend the Charter order as the source of peace, admitting it has delegitimizing flaws (the P5 veto, US impunity) in the global South's eyes. Kourtis shows international institutions (the Mandate, UNSCOP, the Partition Plan) helping build a racial contract, a structural critique of the same order.
  • Conquest and land. They make the nonrecognition of conquest (the Stimson Doctrine, void coerced treaties) the centre of the order. Kourtis tracks land appropriation, settlements he calls illegal (citing the Wall opinion), and the res extra commercium status of seized land.
  • Gaza appears in both. For them, Trump's suggestion of taking Gaza after expelling two million Palestinians is part of the assault, and the Hague Group is working to enforce ICJ and ICC decisions on Gaza. For Kourtis, Gaza is where he locates genocidal activation after 7 October 2023, with the ICJ's provisional measures as evidence.
  • The General Assembly. They want the Assembly to lead (the veto initiative; 142 votes in 2022). Kourtis leans on Assembly practice: Res 96(I), 181(II), 194(III) and 37/123D.
  • Law and power. For them, law works through expectations of enforcement, and a hegemon's defection destroys it. For Kourtis, law itself constructs identities and hierarchies that can prime violence.

Links to other INT301 readings Hathaway & Shapiro

  • Knox, hypocrisy (Wk 2): they write that prior US administrations “can be condemned for their hypocrisy”, the kind of accusation Knox argues is central to international law.
  • Shaw, sources (Wk 3): the prohibition of force is customary law (Nicaragua, GA declarations) and unlawful force is a listed jus cogens example.
  • Charlesworth (Wk 3): her Iraq 2003 example of arguing over sources is one of their erosion cases.
  • Anghie, Chimni (Wk 1): their picture of the pre-1928 order (colonial possessions “won and lost like damages in a lawsuit”, unequal treaties) is the colonial history TWAIL scholars put at the centre.

Links to other INT301 readings Kourtis

  • Mbori, sovereign equality (Wk 2): both argue that racial hierarchy is built into doctrine that looks neutral.
  • Shaw (Wk 3): the Genocide Convention's obligations are erga omnes (Bosnia v Serbia) and genocide is a jus cogens example; Kourtis uses the treaty-interpretation rule on evolving generic terms.
  • Charlesworth (Wk 3): GA resolutions as evidence (Res 194(III) as a “juridical consensus”).
  • Anghie (Wk 1): the mandates system as colonial international law, the foundation of the racial contract.

Before the exam

Quick revision

INT301 quizzes ask who argued what, key terms, cases and treaty articles.

Hathaway & Shapiro in ten lines

  1. Trump's threats (Greenland, Panama Canal, Gaza, Ukraine) are “a cohesive assault” on the prohibition on force.
  2. Before 1928 war was lawful; “it was the order”; war manifestos; Grotius on just war and booty; “might made right”.
  3. Examples: Mexico 1846 (525,000 sq mi for $15m); Perry and Kanagawa 1854; Napoleon on Elba; neutrals could not sanction.
  4. Kellogg–Briand 1928 (58 signatories) outlawed aggressive war; mocked, but it started the modern order.
  5. The Stimson Doctrine (Manchuria 1931): no recognition of conquest or coerced treaties; Nuremberg's first count cited the Pact; Jackson on Lend-Lease reshaped neutrality.
  6. The 1945 Charter codified it: coerced treaties void, neutrality not impartial, aggressors criminally responsible.
  7. Results: over 150 conquests in the century before, fewer than 10 since; no UN member conquered out of existence; states tripled; trade 10% to 58% of GDP; outcasting; checkbook diplomacy.
  8. Law works through expectations of response, especially the US's (Kuwait 1990), not through a sense of obligation.
  9. Trump: gunboat diplomacy, whim tariffs, ICC sanctions, isolationism; the system collapses “piece by piece”.
  10. Fix: admit flaws (P5 veto, US impunity), midsize coalitions, the GA veto initiative, the Council of Europe aggression court, the Hague Group, an “outcasting council”, and outcasting the US itself if needed.

Kourtis in ten lines

  1. The protected groups (national, ethnic, racial, religious) hold a collective right of existence, but “racial group” is undefined.
  2. Thesis: the groups are “dynamic and relational social constructs”, not only permanent and stable ones.
  3. Drafting: Lemkin's genos; race fit the idea of permanence and was used to exclude political groups, liberation movements and colonized peoples; delegates split between biological and ethnonational readings.
  4. A tautology from the motive-based origins: race defines the group and the group is defined by race.
  5. Human rights law: race is a by-product of discrimination. Genocide law: race is the reason for the right to exist. Apartheid law: the oppressors' view prevails.
  6. Three trends (visible traits; perpetrator view; Schabas's 1940s meaning) each fail; generic terms evolve (Costa Rica v Nicaragua).
  7. The racial contract (Mills) is juridified: Balfour and the Mandate erased Palestinians; UNSCOP and partition.
  8. Israeli law, he argues, constitutes the racialized subject: the Law of Return, the Citizenship Law, the Nation-State Law, the Absentees' Property Law, “law of the enemy”, family-reunification bars.
  9. Definition: identity that is “hybrid, situational, fragmentary, and negotiable”.
  10. Priming (racialization etc., “necessary but not sufficient”) leads to activation (architects, abandoned constraints). He places activation after 7 October 2023, calls apartheid a prelude, and concludes that Palestinians qualify for protection and that the evidence shows a “high probability of genocidal intent”.

Terms

War manifesto
A state's published legal case for going to war (old order).
Right of conquest
Seizing land to remedy a wrong; lawful before 1928.
Gunboat / checkbook diplomacy
Coercion by threat of force / by economic means.
Stimson Doctrine
Nonrecognition of territory taken by illegal force.
Outcasting
Excluding violators from the benefits of cooperation (sanctions).
Veto initiative
A vetoed Security Council draft automatically goes to the GA for debate.
Protected tetrad
The national, ethnic, racial and religious groups of art. II.
Racial contract
Mills: the agreements that constitute racial hierarchy; juridified.
Racialized subject
The identity produced by that contract; holder of the right to exist.
Normative phantasm
Butler: race as identification practices, not a natural fact.
Racial Palestinianization
Goldberg: Palestinians made suspect, threatening and foreign.
Double-consciousness
Du Bois: seeing oneself through the oppressor's eyes.
Essentializing / annihilating othering
Hinton: false dichotomies / cleansing an “alien” threat.
Genocidal priming / activation
Conditions raising risk / the trigger that unleashes violence.
Humanity gap
Anderson: the moral distance that enables atrocity.
Dolus specialis
Genocide's special intent to destroy a group in whole or in part.

Traps

  • H&S do not say the US was blameless: Vietnam, Iraq 2003 and counterterrorism rested on over-broad self-defence, and the P5 veto and US impunity delegitimized the order. Their claim is that the US never violated the prohibition on territorial conquest.
  • For H&S, the law works through expectations of others' responses, not internalized obligation.
  • The Pact had 58 signatories in 1928; the Stimson Doctrine answered Manchuria 1931.
  • Kourtis says racialization does not automatically lead to genocide; priming is “necessary but not sufficient”.
  • Apartheid vs genocide differ in intent: sustaining a regime vs destroying a group.
  • Kourtis critiques all three readings of race, including Schabas's, and relies on the rule on evolving meaning.
  • The ICJ order of Jan 2024 concerned plausibility at the provisional-measures stage, as Kourtis states.

Course lens

What is IL, who makes it?
H&S: rules plus institutions plus shared expectations, made by states and upheld by a hegemon until now. Kourtis: law that constructs identities and hierarchies (racial contracts), made by states and international institutions alike.
Power
H&S: power enforced the order, and a hegemon's defection destroys it; they want power shared more widely. Kourtis: power defines race (“about power as much as belonging”) and law mediates domination.
Approach
H&S: liberal internationalist and institutionalist. Kourtis: critical race theory and TWAIL-adjacent critical legal scholarship, with criminology and victimology.

Retrieval practice

Self-test

Blue cards test Hathaway & Shapiro; ochre cards test Kourtis.

H&S Q1Which four Trump moves open the essay, and what do the authors say they amount to?

Threats to seize Greenland and the Panama Canal, the idea of owning Gaza after expelling two million Palestinians, and demanding Ukraine cede territory: “a cohesive assault” on the prohibition on force.

H&S Q2What was the legal status of war before the twentieth century?

Legal, the main way to enforce rights; “it was the order”. War manifestos stated the causes (ship damage, debts, treaty breaches, self-defence); Grotius: a just war executes a right; conquest was presumed just.

H&S Q3Give three historical examples of the old order.

Mexico 1846 (525,000 sq mi for $15m and forgiven debts); Perry and the Treaty of Kanagawa 1854 (gunboat diplomacy); Napoleon's exiles (war not a crime). Neutrals could not sanction belligerents.

H&S Q4What did the Kellogg–Briand Pact do, and why do the authors defend it?

In 1928, 58 signatories renounced war as an instrument of national policy. It failed to stop WWII but started the process that remade international law (nonrecognition, Nuremberg, neutrality, the Charter).

H&S Q5What was the Stimson Doctrine?

After Japan invaded Manchuria (1931), the US refused to recognise land seized illegally, and League members followed; coerced treaties would not be recognised either, so gunboat diplomacy lost its legal force.

H&S Q6How did the Pact change neutrality?

Robert Jackson justified Lend-Lease (1941): an aggressor “acquires no right to equality of treatment from other states”, so neutrals no longer had to be impartial.

H&S Q7What evidence do they give that outlawry worked?

Over 150 conquests in the century before WWII against fewer than 10 since; annual conquest under 6% of before; states tripled; no UN member conquered out of existence; great powers have not openly fought since 1945.

H&S Q8According to them, how does international law shape behaviour?

Through expectations: states behaved because they expected others, especially the US, to respond (Kuwait 1990), not necessarily because they felt they ought to comply.

H&S Q9What replaced war as the means of enforcement?

Economic and diplomatic sanctions (“checkbook diplomacy”) and outcasting, backed by interdependence (trade from 10% to 58% of GDP; 250,000+ treaties) and US economic power.

H&S Q10What flaws in the US role do they admit?

Vietnam, Iraq 2003 and counterterrorism relied on over-broad self-defence claims; the P5 veto; nobody could hold the US to account; the order was delegitimized in the global South. But the US never broke the prohibition on territorial conquest.

H&S Q11List four ways Trump undermines the prohibition.

Threats of conquest; abandoning Ukraine (“losing [his] whole country”, a plan ceding 20%); gunboat diplomacy toward Canada and Mexico; whim tariffs (25%) blunting sanctions; sanctioning ICC personnel; isolationism undermining outcasting.

H&S Q12Why can't Europe simply replace the US?

It lacks the military power, economic influence and political unity, and relying heavily on any single actor would repeat the old mistake.

H&S Q13What institutional fixes do they propose?

Coalitions of midsize and small states (EU model); a stronger GA (193 equal votes; the veto initiative → sanctions, arms, register of damages); regional coalitions (Council of Europe aggression court, Hague Group, AU–EU); an “outcasting council” for automatic joint sanctions.

H&S Q14How do they end the essay?

The system is not self-sustaining; states could outcast the US itself (e.g. over the Panama Canal); developing states risk becoming “the spoils of great-power rivalries”; leaders must design institutions “rather than sit and watch as Trump rewinds the clock”.

Kourtis Q1What gap in genocide scholarship does Kourtis address?

The protected groups, the right-holders of the right of existence, are under-theorized: subjective or objective? how to define each of the tetrad? Race is hardest, being scientifically discredited yet protected in art. II.

Kourtis Q2State his hypothesis.

The four groups are more than permanent, stable and inescapable: they are “dynamic and relational social constructs” with identity linked to both in-group and out-group perceptions.

Kourtis Q3How did Lemkin use race?

From genos (race or tribe): genocide as Nazi Germany's racial masterplan (citing Rosenberg). The idea was cultural and ethnonational but also biopolitical; it set genocide apart from interwar debates and so “de-politicized and essentialized” Nazi criminality.

Kourtis Q4Why did racial groups meet no resistance in drafting, and whom did the same logic exclude?

Race fit ideas of permanence, stability and inescapability; those same ideas were used to exclude political groups, liberation movements and peoples under colonial domination.

Kourtis Q5How did delegates understand “racial”?

Split: biological (Haiti, Norway, Sweden; the UK's “accident of his birth”) against national or ethnic (Egypt, Belgium, Iran, the Netherlands, the USSR; peoples called “races”). Minorities-treaty usage and the framers' practice (Greece 1948, Rusk 1950) point to ethnonational meaning.

Kourtis Q6What is the “tautology” of racial groups?

From genocide's origins as a crime of motive: race defines the racial group and the group is defined by race, so members are targeted by “chance”. It persisted after motive was dropped.

Kourtis Q7How does race differ in human rights law, genocide law and apartheid law?

Human rights: race is a by-product of discrimination (ICERD; self-identification). Genocide: race is the reason for the collective right to exist. Apartheid: race is qualified by the system of domination, with the oppressors' perceptions prevailing.

Kourtis Q8Name the three trends in reading “racial group”, and his objection to each.

Visible traits (Akayesu, Proxmire Act): cannot explain solidarity. Perpetrator-subjective (Lingaas): “Right-holders cannot be hypothesized”. Historical, 1940s meaning (Schabas): assumes fixed referents, shared understanding, and frozen meaning.

Kourtis Q9Which interpretive rule does he rely on?

Generic treaty terms in long-lasting treaties are presumed to evolve (Costa Rica v Nicaragua 2009; Namibia 1971; Aegean Sea 1978), so race is read in today's sense, just as new religious groups are covered.

Kourtis Q10What is the racial contract, and how does it operate in international law on Palestine?

Mills: agreements constituting racial hierarchy, juridified by law. Balfour and the Mandate erased Palestinians as “non-Jewish communities”; UNSCOP and the Partition Plan institutionalized inequality: “idealized racial Palestine”.

Kourtis Q11Which Israeli laws does he say constitute the racialized subject?

The Law of Return and Citizenship Law (“citizen strangers”), the Nation-State Basic Law (sole self-determination), the Absentees' Property Law (four grounds; present-absentees), Basic Law: Israel Lands (res extra commercium), Penal Law art. 91 “enemy”, the family-reunification bars and Knesset art. 7A.

Kourtis Q12Give his definition of a racial group.

“A human figuration whose members are perceived and perceive themselves as having some different characteristics ascribing to them a distinct identity, the latter being hybrid, situational, fragmentary, and negotiable.”

Kourtis Q13Illustrate race as situational, hybrid and negotiable.

Situational: Mizrahi Jews included once an Arab other emerged (Shenhav's “entry ticket”). Hybrid: Knesset art. 7A demands loyalty to the Jewish state. Negotiable: “good Arabs vs bad Arabs”; Kaminsky and Bar-Tal's labels; the Nakba funding law and “forced forgetting”.

Kourtis Q14Distinguish genocidal priming from activation.

Priming: factors (racialization, marginalization, securitization, dehumanization) raising the risk over time; necessary but not sufficient. Activation: leaders (“architects”) exploit an event to present genocide as rational and abandon constraints.

Kourtis Q15How does he apply the framework after 7 October 2023?

He treats the attacks as the activation milestone, given decades of priming and the existential rhetoric that followed (Eiland, Strook, the PM, Barak's opinions), Gallant's “removed all restraints”, and the dehumanizing imagery; he calls apartheid a prelude.

Kourtis Q16What does he conclude, and how does he use the ICJ?

Palestinians qualify as a protected racialized group; conditions are “alarmingly consistent” with genocidal processes; officials' statements show a “high probability of genocidal intent”. The ICJ's January 2024 order used such statements to assess plausibility; incitement matters because genocide is a collective endeavour (Kirsch).

Coverage audit

How both summaries were checked against the texts, and what the first draft missed.

Method

  • Hathaway & Shapiro: both scanned PDFs were OCR'd page by page. The main file stops mid-sentence on p. 92; the file “H and S - Might Makes Unright” holds the final page (p. 93), so the two were combined.
  • Kourtis: the born-digital text was extracted page by page and the OUP download watermark stripped.
  • Headings, cases, instruments, people and years were pattern-matched against this page; every paragraph and sentence was scored for vocabulary overlap, and low scorers were read against the summary.

What the first draft missed

  • H&S: the First World War's “destructive new technologies” and the “desperate search” that followed; Napoleon ruling Elba as a sovereign.
  • Kourtis: the footnoted right-to-exist case list (including Krstić); Kambanda as the source of “crime of crimes”; the formal names of the Gaza case and the Apartheid Convention; the 1958 date of the Knesset Basic Law; the image of priming heat rising towards “an existential precipice”.
  • Removed a journal volume number that was not in the source.

Left out on purpose

  • Kourtis's footnotes that only cite sources (most of his 304); every substantive note is included and marked fn.
  • Foreign Affairs pull quotes, which repeat lines already summarised.
  • Law-report page and paragraph numbers.

Limits of this check

  • It catches missing names, terms and vocabulary better than a subtle misreading, and it was run by the same AI that wrote the summaries.
  • Kourtis's claims about apartheid and genocide are contested. This page reports them as his argument; it does not assess them.
  • Quotations come from OCR (H&S) and extracted text (Kourtis). Check the PDFs before relying on exact wording.
